speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of these, 25 arise from the Financial Year or FY 2020 Budgets and the Ministerial Statement by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance, Mr Heng Swee Keat, on 17 August 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another 14 amendments arise from the periodic review to refine or clarify Singapore's income tax regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have sought views from the public on the draft Bill earlier this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF has evaluated the feedback received and incorporated them where they are relevant to the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 56 of the Bill provides for this amendment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This allows businesses to get a refund of up to $17,000 of income tax paid for YA2017 to YA2019.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 29, 34, 35, 36 and 39 of the Bill provide for this amendment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The scope of the scheme has also been enhanced to cover more qualifying expenses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 17, 19 and 20 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Fourth, to continue encouraging companies to consider mergers and acquisitions or M&A for growth and internationalisation, the M&A scheme has been extended to cover qualifying acquisitions made on or before 31 December 2025.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 41 of the Bill provides for this amendment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Fifth, prescribed payouts received by individuals, businesses and employers under certain schemes announced this year, like the Self-Employed Person Income Relief Scheme, COVID-19 Support Grant and Jobs Support Scheme, will be exempt from income tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will allow citizens and business owners to benefit from the full amount of the support measures, without having to pay tax on them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 16, 22 and 60 of the Bill provide for these exemptions and amendments relating to these exemptions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, as highlighted earlier, MOF regularly reviews and refines the income tax regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, let me now touch on several key amendments amongst those arising from this periodic review of the tax regime which are found in the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, the tax avoidance rules only allow the Comptroller's adjustments to restore taxpayers to their initial tax position, as if the tax avoidance arrangement had not been entered into.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is insufficient to deter aggressive taxpayers from taking the risk of later adjustments made by the Comptroller to counteract the tax avoidance arrangement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a related amendment, we will also amend the Stamp Duties Act to introduce a surcharge equal to 50% of the amount of additional stamp duties payable as a result of adjustments made to counteract the tax avoidance arrangement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 30, 31 and 63 of the Bill provide for these amendments, and a similar amendment is proposed for the Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Bill which we will discuss later.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, to encourage taxpayers to enjoy the convenience of digital services, and to allow them to get refunds faster, MOF will be allowed to prescribe in subsidiary legislation that tax refunds by the Comptroller of Income Tax to companies are to be made via electronic means.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: An assessment of the readiness of companies will be made in 2021, and exceptions will be provided where needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 5 of the Bill provides for this amendment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And a similar amendment is also being proposed for the GST (Amendment) Bill 2020 for refunds of GST by the Comptroller of GST to GST-registered businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, the ITA is amended to clarify the application of the section 37B adjustment factor.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The section 37B adjustment factor should be applied when offsetting any unabsorbed capital allowances, losses and donations in respect of income that is subject to tax at one rate, against income subject to tax at another rate, whether within the same YA or across a different YA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, say there is a $1 million loss arising in respect of income taxed at 10%, the tax savings should be $100,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Without applying the section 37B adjustment factor, this loss will give rise to $170,000 tax savings if it is offset against income taxed at 17%.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But with the section 37B adjustment factor, we ensure that the tax savings from this loss remains at $100,000 regardless of the tax rate of the income it is eventually offset against.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I should clarify there is no change in policy intent or even in practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But this amendment seeks to ensure that the section 37B adjustment factor applies in all scenarios, and it is consistent with existing practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have provided a validation clause to provide certainty that past applications of this adjustment factor were valid, and that unabsorbed capital allowances, losses and donations brought forward from prior years will continue to be preserved at their tax savings value in line with the policy intent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 37, 38, 39, 42 and 66 of the Bill provide for these technical amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have been able to rely on our reserves to supplement traditional fiscal policy during this trying time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, prudence dictates that we not only spend wisely but also carefully examine our revenue streams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is our fiduciary responsibility to Singaporeans to be sound stewards of our nation's fiscal balances and reserve holdings, both today and tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wish to only offer a few brief additional remarks on the general spirit underlying some of the Bill's specificities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Bill seeks to further bolster the longstanding stance of minimising tax avoidance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With Government expenditures heightened as a result of pandemic related spending, assuring the integrity of the revenue side on the balance sheet has become even more imperative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, perhaps additional clarity as to estimates of how much leakage currently exists would be helpful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given the rising trend in self-employment and entrepreneurship, has avoidance become more pervasive over time?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, are there mechanisms other than the more punitively oriented surcharges dealt within this Bill to better nip avoidance in the bud?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps the Minister would be willing to share if tools in artificial intelligence designed to identify anomalous patterns in data on individual tax returns vis-a-vis bank account flows or credit card usage are being deployed to better identify such potential arrears?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Bill also introduces a number of amendments that permit allowances on capital expenditure such as in clauses 15, 27 and 56.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such relief is certainly welcomed, especially by small and medium enterprises who are facing unprecedented challenges in keeping their businesses afloat at this time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, it is worth noting some seeming discrepancies in the applicable duration for capital taxes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clause 40, for instance, indicates that deductions for qualified investments are to have occurred between July 2010 and March 2020.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, allowances in clause 27 are for three years whereas write-offs are for two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This essentially institutionalises differential treatment of capital and labour in the revised tax code.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some justification for this distinction would be very much welcomed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is also useful to observe that the Bill offers extremely limited relief for individual employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clause 16, for instance, provides exemptions for expenditures on accommodation and other necessities for those who normally are residents outside of Singapore but who have, due to COVID-19, been forced to remain here for a year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But there are precious few other cuts applicable for employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, the Budget has stipulated a host of direct transfers that workers enjoy – either directly via cash grants or indirectly through the Jobs Support Scheme, for example.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Academic research also suggests that fiscal policy tends to offer more bang for the buck when effected as spending rather than tax cuts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, a more universal income tax cut may excessively compromise fiscal balances and thereby run at cross-purposes to the targeted transfers effected by the various Budgets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, given the prevalence of COVID-19-inspired income tax reductions in many countries worldwide, it seems fair to question whether there could be room for explicit income tax relief for specific groups within society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will apply in particular to workers within Tier 1 and Tier 2 sectors as discussed previously, such as flight crew and hotel staff for the former, and musicians and restaurant personnel in the latter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given the relatively small size and disproportionately difficult economic circumstances faced by employees in these industries, further tax relief may be especially welcomed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken up previously on our COVID-19 support measures and I am supportive of the increased financial support that we are providing in these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this speech, I will focus instead on another important issue – tax avoidance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill proposes significant changes to strengthen our tax avoidance regime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points to make on these changes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the test for tax avoidance arrangements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The test for tax avoidance is set out in the case of Comptroller of Income Tax versus AQQ, which sets out a scheme and purpose approach for interpreting section 33.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CIT vs AQQ remains the landmark decision for the approach to applying section 33 and has been followed in subsequent cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The IRAS e-Tax Guide on anti-avoidance provisions also states that the Comptroller adopts an approach based on the principles set out by the Court of Appeal in the CIT vs AQQ case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the principles for determining tax avoidance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To determine whether there was tax avoidance, again, CIT vs AQQ requires that the Court look at whether the use of a specific provision in the ITA was within the contemplation of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the bulk of the guidance on what constitutes tax avoidance has been provided by the Comptroller in the IRAS e-Tax Guide or in case law rather than the Parliament's clarification on whether certain uses of the ITA provisions constitute tax avoidance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the arrangements listed in the IRAS e-Tax Guide should be understood as arrangements that the Parliament considers as tax avoidance?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on the comptroller's discretion in pursuing tax avoidance arrangements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the current Act, the Comptroller may disregard tax avoidance arrangements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In response to public feedback that the Comptroller should be allowed to retain discretion on whether to take action against tax avoidance arrangements, the Ministry stated that the amendment is consistent with the strong stance taken against tax avoidance in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I agree with the strong approach against tax avoidance, the new section 33A(7) also provides that the Minister may "for good cause, remit wholly or in part any surcharge or interest payable under this section".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The surcharge here refers to the 50% surcharge that must be paid if a tax avoidance arrangement is found on top of any penalty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The ability of the Comptroller to remit the surcharge or interest appears to be slightly inconsistent with the strong stance we have taken against tax avoidance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Assoc Prof Lim highlighted the different durations in the schemes for the various capital allowances and profits, and I think he also compared it with the time frame for GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Every scheme has to be considered on its own merit – the objective of the scheme, the time frame and then the continuous review of the scheme to ensure that it is relevant and serves its objective.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That applies for each individual revenue scheme, it applies for each individual tax item and it also applies for our overall revenue base.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have to ensure that at the overall level, we have a revenue position that is sustainable in order to meet expenditures on an on-going basis, and that is what we will continue to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On Assoc Prof Lim's comment about tax avoidance, it is an area that we continuously look at – whether or not the leakage exists and has it become more pervasive, it is hard to quantify this but we do know that tax avoidance arrangements are becoming increasingly creative and complicated.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why IRAS indeed uses a range of analytical tools to try and detect such cases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we also need to future-proof our anti-avoidance rules to ensure that taxpayers are sufficiently deterred from entering into such arrangements in the first place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Hence, the amendments that are being proposed here.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, Mr Ng asked if the existing test for ascertaining tax avoidance in the landmark CIT vs AQQ case will continue to apply.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, Mr Ng asked if the examples of arrangements that are provided in IRAS' e-Tax Guide should be understood as arrangements that the Parliament should consider as tax avoidance arrangements.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I should clarify, Mr Speaker, that these tax avoidance arrangements provided in the e-Tax Guide are the Comptroller's guidance to taxpayers on what he considers to be examples of tax avoidance arrangements.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These examples are, in part, distilled from cases to date and are not meant to be and cannot be conclusive or exhaustive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Whether an arrangement constitutes tax avoidance will still have to depend on the facts of the case concerned and then it will go back to the provisions in the Act as well as the provisions in section 33.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A taxpayer who disagrees with the Comptroller's decision may appeal to the Income Tax Board of Review and thereafter, to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, Mr Ng asked if the ability to remit the proposed surcharge or interest payable under this new section 33(A) is inconsistent with our stance against tax avoidance and the circumstances in which surcharge or interest may be remitted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We cannot anticipate what the scenarios will be but in the event that something were to happen that is meritorious, then indeed we will have a remission provision that can be exercised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, whether or not the surcharge or interest on the surcharge will be remitted will depend on the facts of each case, and whether such a remission is sound.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Members would agree that tax avoidance arrangements are, as I highlighted earlier, becoming increasingly creative and complicated.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We need to do more to ensure that our revenue base is protected.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We need to future-proof our anti-avoidance rules to ensure that taxpayers are sufficiently deterred from entering into such arrangements in the first place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we are putting in place the amendments in this Bill.
